title: An app routes one model to several serving backends with no output-equivalence contract between them
problem: I send the same prompt to the same model through two providers for capacity and failover, and nothing anywhere asserts that the two answer the same way, so a defect in one route reaches only part of my traffic and my aggregate metrics stay green.
symptom: A minority of requests degrade while the rest look normal, user reports contradict each other, and dashboards show no incident because the healthy route dilutes the broken one; the bug is only reproducible on a particular backend, batch size or hardware.
why_now: Multi-backend routing became the default in 2025 (same weights served through first-party APIs, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex, plus aggregator gateways on different accelerators), but the tooling grew only a common request SCHEMA, never an output-equivalence GATE, so precision, sampling and routing differences between backends are invisible until users complain.
existing: Provider-abstraction gateways (LiteLLM, OpenRouter, LangChain chat models) normalise the request and response shape, which makes routes interchangeable in code and thereby hides that they are not interchangeable in behaviour.

Static benchmarks and eval suites are run pre-release against one implementation; Anthropic's own postmortem says the evaluations they ran did not capture the degradation users reported, and were run outside true production systems.
Canary deploys catch a route that errors, not a route that answers slightly worse, because there is no per-route quality signal to compare against a reference route.

evidence.title: A postmortem of three recent issues
evidence.quote: Each bug produced different symptoms on different platforms at different rates. This created a confusing mix of reports that didn't point to any single cause.
evidence.note: The vendor's own postmortem names per-backend divergence as the thing that defeated diagnosis. Same model, three serving platforms (first-party API, Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI) on three accelerator families, with impact rates differing by four orders of magnitude between platforms.

evidence.title: A postmortem of three recent issues
evidence.quote: The evaluations we ran simply didn't capture the degradation users were reporting, in part because Claude often recovers well from isolated mistakes.
evidence.note: Direct statement that the pre-existing eval layer was insensitive to a real production regression, which is why the missing primitive is a continuous per-route comparison rather than a better static benchmark.

evidence.title: A postmortem of three recent issues
evidence.quote: Although we run regular evaluations on our systems, we will run them continuously on true production systems to catch issues such as the context window load balancing error.
evidence.note: The remediation the provider committed to is exactly the missing primitive: continuous equivalence measurement on live routes. A consumer of several providers needs the same gate and has no off-the-shelf way to get it.

build_hypothesis: A parity harness with two moving parts: a golden transcript set with assertions that are stable under sampling (schema validity, tool-call shape, refusal or non-refusal, numeric answer, language of the response), and a runner that replays it against EVERY configured backend on a schedule plus a small shadow sample of live traffic, reporting per-route pass rates side by side. The signal that matters is the divergence between routes, not the absolute score, which is why it can be built without a labelled benchmark.

check.manual_question: You reach the same model through more than one serving route (a cloud reseller and a direct or aggregator endpoint). What asserts that the two routes answer equivalently, and would you see it if one route silently got worse for 1 percent of requests?
check.rationale: Two independent route families appearing in shipped code is good evidence of multi-backend serving, and the absence of any parity, equivalence, cross-provider or golden-transcript vocabulary in the test and eval trees is good evidence that nothing compares them. What it can get wrong: a repo may only MENTION a second provider in a comment or an unused config, and a team may run parity checks in an external harness that is not in this repo, which is why a positive result is a signature and not a verdict, and why the mitigation vocabulary is deliberately broad.

bad.app/llm.py:
import boto3
from openai import OpenAI

bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")
direct = OpenAI()

def complete(prompt: str) -> str:
    try:
        r = bedrock.converse(modelId="anthropic.claude-sonnet", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": prompt}]}])
        return r["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"]
    except Exception:
        r = direct.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4o", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
        return r.choices[0].message.content
bad.tests/test_llm.py:
from app.llm import complete

def test_complete_returns_text(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr("app.llm.bedrock", _FakeBedrock())
    assert isinstance(complete("hi"), str)
